questions.q:
The enzyme catalase speeds up this reaction in liver cells:
hydrogen peroxide → water + oxygen
(a) Name the substrate of this reaction. [1]
(b) Name the products of this reaction. [1]
ms: (a) hydrogen peroxide
(b) water and oxygen (both needed)
questions.tip: The substrate is what the enzyme acts on (left of the arrow); the enzyme itself is not a product or a reactant.

questions.q: Describe what is meant by an enzyme–substrate complex.
ms: the substrate fits into / binds to the active site of the enzyme
temporary structure formed (before products are released) / substrate is complementary in shape to the active site
questions.model: It is the temporary structure formed when a substrate molecule fits into the complementary active site of an enzyme, before the reaction happens and the products are released.
questions.tip: Use the key words 'active site' and 'complementary shape'.

questions.q:
A student investigated the effect of pH on a protease from the stomach. She timed how long it took for the protease to digest a piece of egg white.
pH:          1  | 2 | 3 | 5  | 7
time / min: 12 | 5 | 9 | 25 | not digested after 60
(a) State the optimum pH of this protease. [1]
(b) Calculate the rate of reaction at pH 3, using rate = 1 ÷ time. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. [1]
(c) Explain why the egg white was not digested at pH 7. [2]
ms: (a) pH 2
(b) 0.11 per min (min⁻¹)
(c) the enzyme is denatured / active site changes shape
(c) substrate (protein) no longer fits / is no longer complementary to the active site, so no enzyme–substrate complexes form
questions.model:
(a) pH 2, because the shortest time means the fastest rate.
(b) 1 ÷ 9 = 0.11 min⁻¹.
(c) pH 7 is far from the optimum, so the shape of the active site changes and the enzyme is denatured. The protein no longer fits the active site, so no enzyme–substrate complexes form.
questions.tip: Shortest time = fastest rate. Don't read the optimum as the largest number in the time row.

questions.q: A student mixes starch solution with amylase at 30 °C. Describe how she could use iodine solution and a spotting tile to find the time taken for all the starch to be broken down.
ms: put a drop of iodine solution in each well of the spotting tile
remove a drop of the mixture at regular intervals (e.g. every 30 s) and add it to a fresh well of iodine
start the stopwatch as soon as the amylase and starch are mixed
end point: when the iodine stays orange-brown / no longer turns blue-black
record the time of the first sample that stays orange-brown
questions.model: She puts one drop of iodine solution into each well of a spotting tile. She mixes the starch and amylase and starts a stopwatch immediately. Every 30 seconds she uses a pipette to add a drop of the mixture to a new well of iodine. While starch is present the iodine turns blue-black. The end point is the first sample in which the iodine stays orange-brown, and she records this time.
questions.tip: Examiners want a clear end point: 'iodine stays orange-brown', not 'the colour changes'.

questions.q:
The table shows the rate of a reaction catalysed by a human enzyme at different temperatures.
temperature / °C:        10 | 20 | 30 | 37 | 45 | 55
rate / arbitrary units:   4 |  9 | 16 | 20 | 11 |  0
Describe and explain the effect of temperature on the rate of this reaction.
ms: describe: rate increases from 10 °C to 37 °C (with data, e.g. 4 to 20 units)
describe: optimum / maximum rate at 37 °C; rate falls above 37 °C to 0 at 55 °C
as temperature increases (to 37 °C), molecules have more kinetic energy / move faster
more frequent (effective) collisions between enzyme and substrate / more enzyme–substrate complexes formed
above 37 °C the enzyme is denatured / active site changes shape
substrate no longer fits the active site / no longer complementary
at 55 °C all enzyme molecules are denatured (so rate is 0)
questions.model:
The rate increases from 4 units at 10 °C to a maximum of 20 units at 37 °C, which is the optimum temperature. Above 37 °C the rate falls quickly, to 0 at 55 °C.
As the temperature rises up to 37 °C, the enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so there are more frequent effective collisions and more enzyme–substrate complexes form per second. Above 37 °C the enzyme begins to be denatured: its active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits and fewer complexes form. At 55 °C all of the enzyme is denatured, so there is no reaction.
questions.tip: 'Describe' needs the pattern with data; 'explain' needs kinetic energy, collisions, active site shape and denaturation.

questions.q:
A biological washing powder contains a protease from bacteria that live in hot springs. This protease has an optimum temperature of 70 °C.
(a) Egg stains are removed faster when the clothes are washed at 60 °C than at 30 °C. Explain why. [2]
(b) Explain why a protease from the human stomach would not work well in this washing powder at 60 °C. [2]
(c) Only a small mass of enzyme is needed in each wash. Suggest why. [1]
(d) The washing powder removes egg stains but not grease stains. Explain why. [1]
ms: (a) at 60 °C the molecules have more kinetic energy (60 °C is closer to the optimum)
(a) more frequent effective collisions / more enzyme–substrate complexes formed
(b) human enzyme would be denatured (its optimum is about 37 °C) / active site changes shape
(b) protein (substrate) no longer fits the active site
(c) enzymes are catalysts / are not used up / not changed, so can be used again
(d) enzymes are specific: the active site of a protease is complementary to protein, not to fat / a lipase would be needed for fat
questions.model:
(a) At 60 °C, which is closer to the optimum, the enzyme and protein molecules have more kinetic energy, so there are more frequent effective collisions and more enzyme–substrate complexes form.
(b) A human enzyme works best at about 37 °C. At 60 °C its active site would change shape and it would be denatured, so the protein in the stain would not fit.
(c) The enzyme is a catalyst, so it is not used up and each molecule can be used many times.
(d) Enzymes are specific. The active site of the protease only fits protein molecules; grease is fat, which needs a lipase.
questions.tip: Apply your knowledge to the new context: an enzyme's optimum depends on where it comes from.
